utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, The Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good afternoon, Mr. Theunens, to you as well. I would like to remind you again that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you gave at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Kay, are you ready to continue --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber would like to receive at the end of the first part of this afternoon's session an update on the estimates as far as time is concerned, that primarily concerns you, Mr. Kay, and Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: At the end of yesterday's session -- not yesterday's, Friday's session - I referred you to a document, Exhibit D1068, which was a daily report, if you remember. We're going look at the next document I have like that, which is 65 ter 1578.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I haven't addressed this with the court officer yet, but I reviewed the documents I received, but maybe you want to do that another time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Shall I finish this section and then we can go to the others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I leave it your hands when to pay attention to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You can see there this document, Mr. Theunens. It's again another daily report dated the 2nd of September, 1995, exactly the same as the other document that we have seen. It comes from the duty service of the 72nd Brigade, and it is sent to the military police administration in Zagreb but also to other people. That's just the genesis of this document, is the VPU document. We can see there details of situations on the first page concerning crime, reports of what was happening, who was involved. We can notice that it involved officers from Split military police as well as the first police station in a particular municipality. Paragraph 2 is a similar report of crime. If we go to the next page, page 2. Again, we can see the continuation of paragraph 2 concerning that incident. We have another heading similar to the previous document that we looked at at the end of last week, Exhibit D1068. This is violation of provisions of the Code of Military Discipline. Paragraph 1 is a particular incident. Paragraph 2 concerns the Knin military police, and that they were notified by the duty officer of Kistanje police station that a patrol had stopped a vehicle, HV member was transporting goods. A patrol was sent, a man arrested, taken to the Knin military police officers. We can see what he was found with. Page 3 more information from the Knin military police concerning the goods, and it was -- they were confiscated. Misdemeanour report filed. Paragraph 3 is another Knin military police patrol on regular patrol in Kosovo, Knin municipality, soldier stealing goods. We can see that report. A disciplinary report will be filed against him. We see again the headings that were in the previous document. These are obviously pro forma headings that when something fits in, it is included under that heading. My interest is in where this was sent to by the shift leader. We can see there the operations duty department of the military police administration where the document comes from, Military District commander. If we go to page 4, the commander of the Split garrison, number 3, as in the previous report. And the Split security an information service, and then the Court can see the other identities of people to whom it is sent to. I'll read this out once, but it becomes repetitive after more documents: Chief of the Split-Dalmatia police administration, the military court of the Split Military District, military prosecutor's office, assistant commander for operations and training of the 72nd Military Police Battalion, duty officer of the 72nd Police Battalion, chief of the crime military police of the 72nd Police Battalion, and the archives. Again, will you notice that although there was an incident involving the Knin military police, Mr. Theunens, this information from the daily report was not sent to the Knin garrison commander but the Split garrison commander, as the reporting line. Do you have any comment to make on that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honours. As was the case with D1068. Even though there are incidents reported in the zone of responsibility of the Knin garrison commander, he is not included in the addressee list. I cannot say why his name is missing. I cannot say whether he was informed otherwise, but independent of the issue of subordination, it would be normal for the Knin garrison commander or any other garrison commander in whose area an incident that required the intervention of the military police occurred, to be informed one way or the other of this incident as it affects his tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. You'll recollect the matters that I have put to you concerning the fact that Knin garrison was not functioning in the usual manner of a garrison command, because of the circumstances at the time, and I put it to you that that is the reason why this reporting line and the subordination of the military police was not as it was to be expected.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honours, but I -- even after reviewing the other document, I see no reason to change any of the conclusions I drew in relation to the authority General Cermak has over the military police in Knin, as well as the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: May that document be made an exhibit, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, it will be admitted as Exhibit D1069.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1069 is admitted into evidence. Mr., Theunens, may I ask you one additional question in relation to this document and other documents as well. We see that the document is sent to the garrison commander of Split. You have explained to us what the authority was, at least in your view of the Mr. Cermak. Would it be for that same functional authority that the documents which also deal with matters within the area of the Split garrison, would that be the reason why it was sent to the Split garrison command and would it be the only reason as far as you are aware of, that it was sent to that garrison commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours, as I explained, the military police reports here about incidents which occurred or which were caused partly by members of the units of the Split Military District and/or occurred in -- in outside the barracks occupied by units of the Split Military District and as such may affect order and discipline in the garrison area. And that's why they are sent, in my view -- or at least for that reason they are sent to the commander of the Split garrison, and that's also why I would except them to be sent to the commander of the Knin garrison or to have the information that is relevant for these garrison commanders be transmitted to them in another matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You will understand that the -- what I'm trying to find out is whether the Split garrison commander in any respect takes a different position compared to the Knin garrison commander in this respect.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have not seen -- I will rephrase that. I have indeed seen a few documents where we have discussed them that the commander of the Split garrison prior to Operation Storm is concerned about the disciplinary situation in the area of the garrison. He organises, for example, regular meetings with the unit commanders and he forwards the minutes of these meetings to General Gotovina. We have also seen the example where the Split garrison commander uses military police in order to assist him to maintain discipline at a particular occasion. I have not seen such documents, and I mean by this, analysis or reports of meetings of General Cermak with unit commanders or commanders of units located in the area of the Knin garrison, and I have not seen any communication, I mean, written communication between General Cermak and General Gotovina on the disciplinary situation in the area covered by the Knin garrison. So that is, indeed, a difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We're going to look at a few more of these to establish the pattern and then some other relevant documents, and this may assist the Court. Can we look at 65 ter 3191.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And the next few documents are exactly the same, Mr. Theunens, as daily reports. While it's coming up, perhaps you can tell us, did you look at these at the time of your report or before coming to court, before being questioned. Do you know these documents I'm producing?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have a recollection of seeing some of them. Now, I -- I have not systematically analysed them, but I think the point we are discussing now should have been included in my report, i.e., that these reports, which even if -- I mean, which discuss incidents in the Knin garrison are not sent to the Knin garrison commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. That's very fair of you. There were -- there are a large number of these reports on the database untranslated. Have you seen those? I'm picking out the only translated ones there were originally, and then we searched and found more. Did you see untranslated ones per chance?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm -- I must have come across untranslated ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: But have you not under taken any specific action in relation to the untranslated ones --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- of this type. For other documents, I did request at occasion translations, and that was focussed actually on doctrinal documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Again, document here from the military police duty service, 6th of September, 1995, from Split. It's the daily report for the 6th of September, 1995. We see the heading here: Crime, no incidents reported. Violations of provisions of the Code of Military Discipline. We've no need to go into the detail, but we can see on the first line of paragraph 1 here that it's a Knin company, military police case, stopping a vehicle driven by a soldier, that they had come from a house near Knin taken to the military compound. We go to paragraph -- page 2. Page 2, paragraph 2, same date. Another Knin military police company report about an incident at a roadblock involving a soldier, stolen goods. We can see the goods, and they were taken to the Knin police station. 3 is a Split VP. Other incidents listed below. Turn to page 3, we can see another football match here between -- in Zadar, between two clubs and a report on that. 5, Zadar military police were provided security to the match. We can see the other incidents that are listed. Military road traffic security, we can again see a Knin military police company patrol and a traffic accident. And, again, sent to the same people. Number 3 is the Split garrison commander. If we turn to page 4, we can see the identities of the other relevant parties. And I presume your answer is the same as the previous answer.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: May this document be made an exhibit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1070, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1070 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have another 30 or so of these that are in exactly the same format. They're the daily reports. They do not go to the Knin garrison commander. They go to the Split garrison commander. Of these, there was one fully translated -- two fully translated and another two that had partial translations which my team completed for me to make up the rest of the account. The remaining 30 or so documents all remain untranslated documents, but they are for an important feature of the case concerning the reporting of the military police and these Knin company military police incidents. I propose to bar table them with Your Honour's leave unless the Court wants to look at any more such further incidents and to submit the untranslated copies to the translation department so that in the fullness of time, they can produce the translations for the Court. Does that meet with the Court's approval? I can go into more of the documents, but I'm flagging up that the story remains the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You were talking about 30 and 30, but I do understand there are 30. There are two fully translated, two to some extent translated, which means that the remaining 30 or so is the remaining 26 or so. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's a collection here, Your Honour, and I can't count them on my feet. But it is it about that, and they're all flagged up. I have been through every single one and so has my team, and it's exactly the same position with these daily reports going to the Split garrison commander, and they involve the Knin company incidents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You'll understand that the lack of translation is my first concern. Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that they could be marked for identification pending translation. But perhaps we can on the basis of the B/C/S original come to a type of agreement [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I wondered whether the parties could stipulate that these are similar type of reports covering also events that happened within the Knin garrison command area of responsibility, but nevertheless, although sent to the Split garrison commander, not been sent to the Knin garrison command. If the parties could agree on that, then I don't think we have to admit all of them in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I leave it to the parties. Otherwise, I would follow the suggestion by Mr. Waespi; that is to say, they will be marked for identification, we'll wait for translation so that then the other party could review them and see whether they really are the same kind of documents and then finally decide upon admission. But it saves the effort of translation, if the parties would agree on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. And we will have saved an hour and a half or an hour of Court's time by taking this, which is my main concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The parties are invited to report to the Chamber whether any stipulation could be made.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Your Honour, it's not the Prosecution's fault that they're untranslated or -- they're just in the database, and we've done a considerable research to get them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I did not understand your remarks as blaming the Prosecution for not having translated something they did not intend to use. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I raised it with Mr. Waespi last Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just taking this up, there are a couple of other documents that need to be looked at in this context, Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we, first of all, go do Exhibit D47.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is a document dated 14th of August, 1995, and I believe you're familiar with this document, Mr. Theunens. It's in your report.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We can see it's from the military police administration to the battalions of the military police, including the 72nd and 73rd, implementation of military and police tasks. It refers to the order of the 2nd of August, ending 466 that we looked at earlier and you looked at with Mr. Misetic. We've no need to go back to that for this exercise. We can see the description at this date that the commander of the -- chief of military police administration, General Lausic, who issued this document, is referring to about the completion of Oluja, the units of the military police. They were organised in line with the order of the 5th of August, 1995. They took operational zones of responsibility during the operation. They took over zones of responsibility which weren't in line with a particular directive, obviously for operational reasons, and then based on the above, with the aim of performing military and police tasks efficiently and effectively, an order is made, which we've no need to go through all the provisions in detail as they won't apply and are not relevant for these purposes, but I'm aware you will know what item 1 of 466 is, as I do, concerning combat readiness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we go to the next page, which concerns in paragraph 2, reserve units being mobilized.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Paragraph 3, he invalidates from the earlier order, leaving it up to the commanders of the military police units to decide when they will abolish their forward command posts of battalions and companies. We can see other sequential orders invalidating that order of 2nd of August, which puts the military police on awareness for combat operations. We've no need to look that in detail. If we go to page 3, paragraph 8 states that military and police tasks shall be carried out by foot and motorised patrols, independently as well as together with the police. 9 is about check-points. Further check-points in 10. And relationships between the 73rd and 72nd. No need to go further in that. If we look at page 4, the last page, paragraph 14: "Normalize the command and control structure. Cover the entire zone of responsibility in daily reports through the duty service." Those are the reports we have just been looking at, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is likely that these are the reports. I cannot be 100 percent sure, but it is likely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We've seen those reports headed "Duty Service."

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... and daily reports of what the duty service provide.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And in separate reports on incidents in the newly liberated area of the state, supply a separate report on the mopping up of the terrain in encoded version or by courier. And then in the daily operative command subordinate the commanders of the newly established platoons and companies of the Knin military police to the most senior commander. Provide daily reports to these commanders and to the Croatian armed forces in the zone of responsibility. Just to let you consider that.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether the last text you read out is identical or what I see in paragraph 14 at the end of the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I've read the English. Maybe the translation booth can just translate the last two sentences of paragraph 14 from the Croatian on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "In the daily operations command, the commanders of the newly established platoons and companies of the Knin military police shall be subordinated to the most senior commander of the HV in the area of responsibility and shall submit daily reports to them."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I think the gist of it was in the English in the original.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Except a different order of words.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If I can thank the translation booth helping us out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You also know, Mr. Kay, that is more or less against the rules that we ask translations by the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hope they will forgive you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So looking at that, first of all, it's right, isn't it, there is not within the evidence a single report from the Knin company of the military police to General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not seen a written report by the Knin military police company to General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. That's an exhibit already. We can see who this document is sent to, signed by General Lausic, and I now wanted to continue this with an order two days later that follows on from this document, which is ending in number 530.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: May we have Exhibit P878 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is an exhibit dated the 16th of August, 1995. We can note the number there that it ends in 538 as this will continue through. It's sent to all military police units and military police administration departments and sections by General Lausic from the military police administration, and it's order on the implementation of military police tasks. We can see the reference there to that order we have just been looked at, dated 14th of August, and the one we have previously been familiar with, dated the 5th of August and ending in 485. And it says: With the change in the deployment of Croatian army units in the newly liberated areas of the Republic ... and organisation, on page 2, of police administrations, police stations of the MUP, conditions have been created for a change in the deployment of units of the military police, and it is ordered and we can see the 69th, 67th, 71st are given various orders on that page. We have no need to look at that in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we turn to page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: At paragraph 5, there's an issue of the standard of appearance, conduct, and equipment of military policemen. And 6 and 7, we need to look at carefully. "In all zones of responsibility, ensure that commanders of military police units are familiar with the deployment of Croatian army units on the line of defence and at camp sites, the strength of the units, the time and direction of redeployment or departure of military police units from the zones of responsibility and that they have the telephone numbers of the commander and vice versa, thus ensuring knowledge of the zone of responsibility on the basis of which the engagement of military police patrols shall also be planned?" And in 7: "By means of military police patrols ... enable the effective implementation of military police authority, work out a schedule for patrols ..." Next page. Paragraph 9, sending the code names of the commanders and duty services of the newly organised military police units, report changes in channels. And at 10: "I make the commanders of military police units responsible for the implementation of this order, and while supervision of its implementation and expert assistance shall be provided by officers of the military police administration departments ..." And we can see, actually, that Split Military District is missed off and is not on, and this would not have been sent to the list of those to receive this particular order. But you see the purpose of this order from General Lausic is that there be contact with the VP units with the telephone numbers of commanders of units, so that there be contact with them. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is one of the instructions General Lausic gives to the addressees of this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. This order comes into the chain for -- because it is referred to later on. If we now go to Exhibit P877. This again is from the military police administration, General Lausic, issuing it to the military police battalions, including the 71st and 72nd, to the commander of those battalions. It's the order on implementation of tasks, efficient cooperation, and you can see the reference there to the three orders that we have looked. First of all, 530 of 14th of August ; 485 of the 5th of August that we looked at last Friday; and 538 of the 16th of August, the last document that we looked at. And you can see on the first page that there are reports to the military police administration of houses being burned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: May we turn to page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That paragraph continues with the reports of crimes being committed by soldiers and civilians wearing Croatian army uniforms on a daily basis, and there's been a communication about cooperation between military and civilian police that has not yielded results, and there have been protested from foreign ambassadors, et cetera, and an order is issued. And it says: "The commanders of military police platoons, companies, and battalions are immediately required to get into touch with the commanders of police stations and chiefs of police administrations in their respective areas and to do the following at a joint meeting ..." And it's a meeting to prevent crime. Page -- paragraph 2: "The commanders of military police platoons, companies, and battalions are required to get in touch immediately with the most senior Croatian army commander in their zone of responsibility, and to implement item 6..." of the order we've just looked at, and to remind you of that it is to ensure that commanders of military police are familiar with the deployment of Croatian army units, have contact details, and they have knowledge of the zone of responsibility so that they can plan patrols. Point 3: "Compile records (notes) about meetings held with commanders of police stations and the chiefs of police administrations pursuant to item 1, and about meetings held with Croatian army commanders pursuant to item 2 of the order and clearly specify the conclusions reached at the meetings. "The records from the meetings should be gathered in the commands of battalions (independent companies), and once compiled, they should be submitted to the military police administration by 8.00 in the evening on 19th August 1995." And in 4: "Immediately submit a ... report ... about lack of cooperation." This document goes -- doesn't go to the Knin garrison. If we turn to page 3, we can see the addressees of the document. So, again, it's same question that have I asked you before, and it is that there is no record of meetings of this nature under point 3 of General Lausic between the Knin company or the 72nd Battalion with General Cermak. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would just like to clarify the addressee list. There is no garrison commander included, because one would expect that such an order by General Lausic to the military police units would be forwarded by the Military District Commanders to their garrison commanders as well as other subordinate units. To answer the question, I have not seen any written reports of meetings between General Cermak and members of the 72nd Military Police Battalion, including the Knin Company, even though while checking the documents you provided me, I came across not really diaries, but type of log-books where reference was made to meetings, or these were personal notebooks where reference was made to meetings, but, like, in one notebook I saw the name "Cermak" only twice, whereby I would expect such meetings to happen on a more regular basis. Maybe this person only attended the meetings twice or there is another reason. I mean, I can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was Cermak's name mentioned rather than a meeting with him. It was just mention of his name?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was actually mention of his name and he giving an instruction but just one line on -- on -- I think there was one for a particular patrol or one for particular check-point. Anyway, that is what I came across this morning when doing searches on the names included -- list of names of commanders included in the duty rotation documents you provided me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. So in these orders here, there is not even the equivalent order from the Split Military District commander to General Cermak applying this point 3 as a system of command and reporting.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not seen any follow-up order by the commander of the Split Military District in relation to this order. I mean, to none of his subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. And this was an exhibit already. And then the last document in this chain is 65 ter 1879.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I just add that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I have connected the P877 it my report to D48, the letter by Mr. Moric to General Lausic, in which Mr. Moric complains about the ongoing burning and other crimes by people in uniform. And this is it on English page 229, part 2 of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Wrong document, I'm afraid. We will just do a little bit of research to my right on this document. The numbers were in the wrong order. 65 ter 1789. Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Mak. This is dated the 19th of August. It is from the 72nd Military Police Battalion. It is sent to General Lausic. I can tell you that on the last page it's from the commander, Mihael Budimir, Major Budimir, and it concerns as we can see in the heading "full implementation of military police tasks in the liberated area," and it refers to the order 547 of the 18th of August, 1995, which is a document which references to the footnote you've just referred concerning cooperation between the MUP, and a report is filed in the 72nd, in paragraph 1, he reports to General Lausic that coordinating meetings were held with Mr. Radalj of the Split-Dalmatia administration. Major Sipcic was present. Check-points being agreed. He refers to Sinj coordinating meeting between Bilobrk, Commander and Captain Jenic of 5th Company. And 3, coordinating meeting with the Sibenik police administration, and details on that. Let us turn to the last page, page 3, and look at paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: "Coordinating meeting was not held in Zadar-Knin police administration because, according to Mr. Cetina, head of the police administration, he had orders to establish contact at the level of command of the 71st and 72nd Military Police Battalion, and no orders on establishing contact at lower levels. Also, he said, he would organise a meeting at the level of commands of these two military police battalions, which carry out military and police tasks in the territory of the police administration." Again, can you see that, that the Knin -- Zadar-Knin police administration was operating or wanted to operate at the level of the command level of the 72nd Battalion, which would have been Major Budimir himself. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And, again, there's no mention in these coordinating meetings of parties and who is to be involved that in that area, which includes Knin, that General Cermak was the party to hold such meetings on behalf of the military police with the police.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: 65 ter 1789 which is discussed on English page 230, part 2 of my report, is the response by Major Budimir to the instruction Lausic included in P877, where he ordered the military police battalion commanders to have meetings, on one hand, with the civilian police, on the other hand, with the HV commanders in the area, and to inform him, i.e., Lausic, of the results of these meetings, and so this 65 ter 1789 only covers meetings between military police and civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: May this document be made an exhibit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1071, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1071 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. And then the last document we'll look at this just to round it off - we could go further down the chain but I'm giving a snapshot of the relevant matters - is 65 ter 2534.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is a document dated the 30th of August, 1995, and it's from General Lausic to the military police battalions, including 71st, 72nd, 73rd. And it concerns these coordination meetings you've just referred to, Mr. Theunens. And in the aim of having them more effective cooperation, and he makes an order based on the 18th of August document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we can turn to page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The -- after successfully carrying out Storm, military police units except for the 68th, established full military and police control over their areas, the commanders of these military police units are responsible for maintaining public law and order, crime control, and security of road traffic for members of the Croatian army, they will ensure these tasks are carried out by executing the authority of the military police working in close coordination with commanders of police stations, chiefs of police administrations. He refers to the other orders that they regulated the obligation to conduct coordination meetings with commanders of police stations and chiefs of police and make joint reports. And then in this order, commanders of the military police units shall determine the level of coordination. They've got to cooperate. If we turn to page 2, we can see that paragraph 2 that the daily exchange of daily reports, an unobstructed system of communications between duty services and prompt response following a call. In 4, that commanders of military police battalions and military police independent companies are responsible for failure to hold cooperation meetings or failure to have effective and practical cooperation. Just dealing with this order, Mr. Theunens, it's right to say, is it not, that, in fact, a very structured system of reporting as well as duties were issued by General Lausic to the commanders of the military police battalions?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed. And that is actually also discussed in my -- in part 2 of my report, where I address the orders issued by General Lausic prior to the launching of Operation Storm. This particular document here, 65 ter 2534, I have addressed at English page 231 of part 2 of the report, and I see it more in light of the -- what one could call ongoing complaints by Mr. Moric and other civilian police officials about what they call a lack of military police cooperation in combatting the crimes that are still being committed in the area that was recaptured during Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. To summarize that information, and there are a large number of orders. We're not going to go through every single one. They are detailed in your report. Others have been in evidence here. They indicate, do they not, that these were exceptional times for the military police, in relation to the need to exercise their duties.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you mean by the word "exceptional." But when you look at the documents and not only the military police documents but also documents, for example, Split Military District, one can see that problems that are observed from the very beginning, i.e., the burning and looting and other examples of lack of discipline continue to be reported notwithstanding various orders to the operational commanders through the operational chain of command as well as to the military police, both via the operational chain, as well as via the professional chain, but nevertheless these problems continue to be observed, and, for example, here I believe this document, yeah, this is from the 30th of August, so almost three weeks after the conclusion of Operation Storm. And that -- I don't want to call or use the expression "exceptional," but that is unusual from the military context, at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It also progresses as we were able to see when Mr. Misetic questioned you last week, or the week before, my apologies, to the meeting in Plitvice, where the Ministry of Interior, military police administration, had what was, in fact, a second meeting, in relation to the crimes that had been continuing within the previously occupied areas. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you just remind me of the date of the Plitvice --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That's 16th of September. We can ...

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have a reference to a meeting in Zagreb on the 15th, which is on English page 237 and that is Roman V, and it is a typo. It should be 15, instead of 16th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You'll recollect you looked at this with Mr. Misetic. It arose because General Lausic made a statement, a public statement, that the military police and civil police were responsible for the prevention of crimes.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed. I remember --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was it the Jezerici. Pardon my expressions. I'm known as a not very able linguist but J-e-z-e-r-i-c-i Hotel in the Plitvice Lakes.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember seeing document, yes, I mean, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's significant because at that meeting there was the commanders of the police administrations, including Mr. Cetina and Mr. Romanic. There was General Lausic. It's Exhibit D595, and, apologies, the meeting was held on the 15th, and if you'd just like to look at this document while here, Exhibit D595.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have in my report on English pages 237 to 239.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Part 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We can see -- this is, in fact, the second meeting. There had also been one here in August, on -- around the 18th of August that preceded this, and there had also been a meeting of the military police in Knin on the 13th of August. If we look at Exhibit D595, coordination meeting, representatives of MUP. We're looking at the military police administration notes.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Sorry, Jezero. My mistake. And we can see Mr. Moric, Mr. Benko, Mr. Lausic, Biskic, heads of the military police battalions, page 2. Mr. Moric is discussing crimes, measures taken against perpetrators, and then each of the police administrations gives a report. We can see Mr. Cetina there. Page 3, chief of Knin police administration and the others' report. Page 4, Colonel Budimir. I have been referring to him as Colonel and Major because the documents say Major as well in their translation, but it's the same individual. He gives a report for the 72nd, saying that there was a large area of responsibility, didn't agree about their not being enough manpower. He was satisfied with security, public order, road traffic safety and refers to disposal of rubbish. Other police commanders. We can see at page 5, General Lausic concluded the reports of his commanders and said: "Members of the MUP and the military police are the promoters of the state policy and the only people responsible for its implementation are present at this meeting. The objective is clear: Protection of people and property and creation of positive security ..." Commanding well ... and cooperation among civilian and military police, he describes, is visible only on the ground. It's necessary to coordinate the communication system, and he had visited the terrain necessary to identify units in certain areas of responsibility, find out everything about them. "That is a duty of the patrol that must detect the HV unit ..." Page 6, Mr. Benko agreed with the need to exchange information, cooperate with courts. Mr. Moric didn't wish to shift responsibility and supported the remarks by General Lausic and said that everybody is engaged in looting from civilians to representatives of civilian authorities, et cetera. The Court has seen this document before. And in page 7 Brigadier Biskic commenting on the minutes to General Lausic states he is not satisfied with them. The notes were not taken accurately, and he suggests they stay only in our archives, and we don't send it to anybody. Right, have I done a lot of talking of this, setting the -- the scene for what is a big subject, but what I'm say something this. When I use the words "exceptional," this is not ordinary times of regular military policing, is it, we are discussing crimes on a large scale, reports of housing being burnt, people being killed, property taken. This is it not crime on a large -- on an ordinary scale, is it?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is it not crime on an ordinary scale, but I think that the -- the statement General Lausic makes here on the 16th reflects his, I would say, state of despair more than a month after the ending of Operation Storm, and after, as I said, a lot of orders being issued both -- I mean, not only both but the chief of the Main Staff in order to have the operational commanders maintain or restore discipline, prevent burning, prevent looting. We see that these orders are going forwarded throughout chain of command, that these orders are often repeated. We see, as I mentioned also orders to the military police through the two chains, and still, 16th of -- excuse me, 15th of December, it appears there is -- that there is no significant improvement in the situation. I mean, I could continue here. We have seen another document, I think it was an analysis by General Lausic on the use of the military police during and after Operation Storm. These documents show what is already explained in the doctrine, that is, that the commander, i.e., the operational commander, is the first one who is responsible for maintaining discipline. And we can see that in Article 4 of D32, the service regulations. That's where it starts. And, of course, military police can be called to assist. Civilian police can be called to assist. But they are not the first who can enforce discipline in the units because it would mean that you would -- would need to have many more military policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. But General Lausic has a responsibility to make his command of the military police effective, doesn't he?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And Major or Colonel Budimir, commander of the 72nd, has his duty to make his command of that battalion effective, doesn't he?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: These duties apply to all commanders, independent of the type of unit or the level they're operating at. It's from the highest to the lowest level and independent of the type of unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. So whatever responsibility other people have, just looking at the military police, that's their job. They're there for that very reason, is to enforce discipline and prevent crimes being committed by the forces. Isn't that right? That's the whole purpose of their job.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The job of the military police or the duties of the military police are specified in Article 10, and enforcing discipline or restoring discipline -- I'm sorry. It was Article 10 of P880, the 1994 military police rules. Enforcing discipline is included in these tasks. However, with the -- how would I explain that? However, keeping in mind, I'm sorry, that military discipline is one of the -- I will call it, core duties of the operational commander. He is the first one who is responsible, and it's only when there are significant incidents or when the operational commander fails to fulfil his duties that it's only then that the military police as well as the military justice system, and military discipline system, of course, I mean, the further steps intervene.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And they are also to be deployed as a presence to prevent crime, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. The deployment of military police should have a deterring effect. Or the presence of military police should have a deterring effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. That deals with this section.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, may 65 ter 2534 be made an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1072, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1072 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And the next thing I was going to turn to having finished this subject is for you to comment on the documents that you wanted to, Mr. Theunens, before we move to another section of the military police. If you want to make that comment now. Is it possible in the next two minutes? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Oh, sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see a reference to the 16th of December in page 27:21 which is not clear it me. And still the 16th, excuse me 16th of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I said September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I take it that was the 15th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the correction was from the 16th to the 15th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So mistake hardly ever comes along, so now we have the 15th of September as the relevant date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I reviewed these documents. With the exception of two documents I can discuss later, they all -- they're all internal military police documents covering the rotation of the members of the Knin company as well as traffic police and even -- and also members of the criminal police from the time-period mid of August 1995 to November 1995. As I explained earlier, when Mr. Kay asked me questions about these documents, these are, in my view, internal military police documents which are only sent through the military police chain. So there is no reference made to operational commanders or garrison commanders or anyone else outside the military police chain. There was one document -- I don't know whether I have to identify it or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What I suggest.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What I suggest is the following: That you give the two numbers so that Mr. Kay can look at these documents during the next break. And then perhaps after the break, Mr. Kay, you can invite the witness to give comments on those documents once he has given you the numbers and once you have been able to focus during the break on these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If could you give the numbers.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first one is 2D07-0099. And the second is 65 ter 5631, which is footnote 968 in part 2 of my report. I don't think I have to comment on that last document in addition, but I just wanted to highlight it was not a rotation document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that's all you wanted to add that, then we have dealt with that one. May I take it, then, that after the break that you will invite the witness to give his comments on 2D07-0099.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Theunens, first of all, thank you very much for having reviewed these documents over the weekend. I'll ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom because I'd like to hear from the parties information on other matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, I invited the parties who have not yet finished their cross-examination to give the Chamber an impression as to how matters stand at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I anticipate I will be able to finish by the end of the next session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then looking at you Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. In that case I will start today in the last session, and I will be -- and I will need probably the whole day tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And your initial assessment was --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was one day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And that will be one day plus one session that Mr. Kay kindly left for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Which, of course, gives a different impression on time taken. Mr. Waespi, how much time would --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Very limited, less than 15 minutes at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Less than 15 minutes. Mr. Misetic, you're on your feet as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In light of some answers that the witness has given in the last 15 minutes, I would need no more than 15 minutes of re-cross, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you are already -- I think we have -- there was a witness who is supposed to appear on Thursday morning where we cannot that easily change, Mr. Waespi. Could you give us an explanation also as to the schedule for the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. This is correct. He -- perhaps we go into private session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. We will have a break and resume at quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, before I give you an opportunity to put the document the witness indicated to the witness, I'll first give an opportunity to the witness to clarify an answer he has given on Friday. At least I was informed, Mr. Theunens, not knowing what it was about, that there was one answer of last Friday you would like to clarify.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. This has to do with the questions by Mr. Kay about the appointment of members of the 72nd Military Police Battalion to ensure the personal protection of General Cermak, which corresponds with pages 13268 and 13269 of the transcript. Mr. Kay showed D770, and I explained why I considered regular that the military police administration actually ordered the 72nd Battalion to ensure this kind of protection to General Cermak. I think we need to put D770 in context, and that context is given by P882, which is referred to in footnotes 901 and 902 of the second part of my report, English page 221. P882 is a report by General Lausic about the activities of the military police units, and on the English page 4, we see an entry, according to which, four members of the 66th Military Police Battalion have been assigned to ensure the personal protection of General Cermak. I don't have the date with me of P882, but I think it is the 6th of August. The 66th Military Police Battalion is a unit which is directly subordinated to the Main Staff of the Croatian armed forces, and that can be found in 65 ter 2889, which is discussed in part 1 of my report. The reason why I think it's useful to clarify D770, because, based on 65 ter 2889, there are members of the 66th Military Police Battalion who, until 22nd of August, i.e., the date of D770, ensure the personal protection of General Cermak, and then this duty is handed over to the 72nd Military Police Battalion, and taken into account the level of units we're talking about, and as I mentioned, the specialized nature of the task, it is logical that it is a member of the military police administration who issues the order for the handover. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Shall we bring up 2D07-0097, which was one of the bar table documents submitted, and after this exercise we'll remove from that and make it an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's a document dated the 25th of October, 1995. It's from the then-commander --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, I'm a bit confused. I see on the transcript from before the break, that reference was made one time by you, and I repeated that from the transcript, and that was 0099, last four digits. I do not know whether this creates any confusion, whether the confusion was before the break or now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That's the English number, and I have been given the Croatian number, I believe. Yeah, it's the same document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Numbers in different languages are the same, in my view, but I do understand it is a reference to a document in Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We will confirm it with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is this the document you were referring to, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed. And I read out the number that is in the bottom right corner on the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah. This is dated the 25th of October, 1995. It's from the commander of the Knin police station at that time, Zvonko Gambiroza, from the Zadar-Knin police administration, as we can see. It's addressed to the commander of the 72nd Military Police Battalion in Knin, and it's the request for an interview of two Croatian army soldiers who'd been noticed in a farm house in Podinarje, or near it, and a fire was noticed and asking the military to conduct interviews with those two soldiers. And in the second page, we can see the information that was given from a Milan Konforta, and obviously of the 7th Knin police station, and giving the details. Mr. Theunens, you wanted to make a comment.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. The only reason why I highlighted this document is that it is a different document from the other ones in the package, i.e., all the other documents, expect for the second one which we discussed before the break, deal with the rotation of military policemen in Knin, whereas this deals with the civilian police requesting the military police to interview two members of the HV in relation to the setting on fire of a house. That was the only reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We knew that, and, actually, we were using that bar table as a clearing up mechanism to reduce documents that didn't require your commenting any further on them, as you knew you wouldn't have a comment on this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, you expected -- at least you saw all the other documents to be of a certain kind, and you just noticed now that at least this one is not of a similar kind as the other one, although Mr. Kay may see similarities on which you may not have focussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And Mr. Waespi and I will be dealing with matters through the usual channels.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's fine. We've dealt with the document. I take it that you -- as you indicated, you don't want to tender it or leave it as a bar table.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We'll leave it with the bar table and not confuse matters, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll turn to another section now, which involves criminal reports of the 72nd Military Police Battalion, Knin Independent Company.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we look at the first document, Exhibit D58, your footnote 1554, and if it helps, 65 ter 2681. This document has been exhibited, and there are about another 20 like it, Mr. Theunens. I think you recognise this document as it's in your report. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. We have been through the 65 ter list and other sources of documents to collect these together into a package of about 20. They are the criminal reports from the Knin company, dated the 5th of September, the first one. It goes to the Split Military District military prosecutor's office. We can see the substance of -- of the report against a man called Burazer, apologies again, B-u-r-a-z-e-r, and if we turn to page 2, it states there, reasonable grounds that he had committed -- suspecting he committed the crime of aggravated theft. It says: "Method of execution." I think it means how the offence was committed rather than anything else, and what was to be stolen. We go to page 3, we see the Knin Military Police stopped him in the area of Knin at 1610, took this man into custody. The goods that he'd been suspected of stealing were stored, and Colonel Budimir sends this to the military prosecutor's office at Split Military District. So a Knin Company report, not sent to the garrison commander, to General Cermak. Any comment that you'd like to make on that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, in my view, this is a report which is -- as Mr. Kay already pointed out when he read out the translation, method of execution, this is a type of report between military police and military prosecutor. It would be logical that the military police has also had contacts with the unit of the person who is subject of this report, and this may include contacts or exchange of information with the garrison commander. But as I said earlier, I have not seen any documents by the military police on crimes being sent to General Cermak. I have only included in my report, I think, one or two reports by the chief of the civilian police which were sent to General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. This document is already an exhibit, Your Honour. We will look at just two more, and then I will, as is the practice now, which I think meets Your Honours' approval, bar table the rest of exactly identical documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, with the proviso that either the witness has an opportunity to check whether it is a similar kind of document or that you and Mr. Waespi agree on the similarity of these kinds of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have 65 ter 2260.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is a similar criminal report, again from the Knin Company of the military police, Mr. Theunens, set out in the same way. It's at your footnote 1554 again, so it's the second document you cite. It concerns a criminal report against an individual. We can see that's it's filed against him on the first page, who he is, what he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we turn to page 2 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We have now the suspicion that he committed a crime of aggravated theft in Golubic, Knin. This time manner of commission. We can see that it's in the Knin area, and he was arrested by Knin military police, taken to their premises under escort. Goods stored there. Page 3, we can see there that it's signed by Colonel Budimir, and again, it is not a document that is referenced to General Cermak. Am I right to say that your answer for this document will be the same as the last?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: May this document be made an exhibit, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is will be Exhibit D1073.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1073 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We shall just do one more. It's at your footnote 1552. It's 65 ter 2262. And I do this so that there's a body of evidence about it, Your Honour, in the transcript, which maybe helps the parties and the Court. Another one dated the 7th of September, 1995. Again from the Knin Company. Criminal report, Split Military District, military prosecutor's office. We can see there the soldier against whom this report is filed against.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Taking an issue here, we know that Colonel Budimir is the commander of the 72nd. Isn't that right, Mr. Theunens?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mihael Budimir is the commander of the 72nd Military Police Battalion, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. He is filing this document on behalf of the Knin Company of the military police, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And it's the same procedure as was with the two previous documents you showed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. And he is filing this document instead of the commander of the Knin company who, at this time, was lieutenant Orsulic?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether it was up to the company commander or the battalion commander to file these reports with the military prosecutor's office, so I can't answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. If we just look at page 2, we can see what he is suspected of doing in the Knin area, aggravated theft. We can see the goods. And on page 3, we can see that the goods were brought to the premises of the military police Knin Independent Company, except for the two sheep, apparently. And on page 4, it's signed by Colonel Budimir. And would it be right that your answer, in relation to this document and the General Cermak question, would be the same as your answer to the first?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And of interest in the overall context is that the alleged perpetrator is described as a displaced person or former displaced person who is a member of the 134th Home Guard Regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, may this document be made an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1074, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1074 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will be bar tabling the rest of this file in due course, and Mr. Waespi and I will be liaising. Can we go to 2D07-0039.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: 2D07-0039. Oh, we don't have it. Okay. All right. If we don't have it, we don't have it, but -- and it's one we can put into the bar table and deal with that way with Mr. Waespi. Oh, we do have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We have it -- I'm sort of staring at that time in e-court myself, so ... if I've got it, everyone else must have it, I should imagine. Have we got it now? There we have it. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: A slightly different document but another report, and it's from -- it's signed by a staff-sergeant Runjic, R-u-n-j-i-c, of the 72nd Military Police. We can see it's a report to Lieutenant Orsulic, the commander of the Knin company of the 72nd. He is reporting on work of the crime military police pursuant to his verbal order of the 11th of September 1995 and in conjunction with the report on work of the crime military police and submitted criminal reports. And he says: "We have delivered you a list of reported cases," which he sets out, and says: "These criminal reports were filed in the premises of the crime military police of the Knin independent company." And the next page he signs it. Any comment you would like to make on this document, Mr. Theunens?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe if I could see the bottom of the page. No, I mean, it's -- the author, he responds to a verbal order as received from his company commander, and he provides him with the requested information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: May this document be made an exhibit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1075, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1075 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. That concludes these questions on these matters. And the next matter I would like to go to is the civilian police but in an a very general way, as we have already looked at a number of Mr. Moric's documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And I'd like to put this matter to you, first of all. Do you agree that the Ministry of the Interior had a -- an organised and hierarchical structure in which subordinates reported to their superiors within the MUP?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And it can be found also in part 1 of the report. There is a structure for the police as well as for the special police whereby we have a -- various bodies existing at different levels from -- from top to bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Shall we see Exhibit P962, where we see this structure from the minister of interior, Mr. Jarnjak, going through Mr. Gledec, down to the assistant ministers, and we have already looked at a number of these names during our questions, Mr. Moric, Mr. Zidovec, Mr. Cemerin, C-e-m-e-r-i-n, Mr. Djurica, Mr. Cetina there in Zadar-Knin police administration. We've seen some of those names in the documents that we've looked at, going down to Mr. Romanic, Mr. Gambiroza, and then down to the police stations on the ground. Do you agree there are no reports from the Ministry of the Interior, from these MUP officials, to General Cermak?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is the question about when we look at the various levels, is the question about the level of the Ministry of Interior, or does the question also cover the civilian police office, Kotar-Knin police administration headed by Cedo Romanic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah. Mr. Romanic there reporting on crimes or his duties to Mr. Cermak, General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have included in section 3, i.e., the section on the Knin garrison command, a few examples of reports on crimes Mr. Romanic sends to General Cermak, but my understanding from the documents is that Mr. Romanic sends this information to Mr. Cermak -- to General Cermak following a request of the latter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Exactly. Yeah. I'm glad you put that way because it shortened matters considerably, and those are documents that we are aware of that a report or inquiry was made, and Mr. Romanic replied in those terms. If we look at 65 ter 3500, we can see an example of this, which is Exhibit D487.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And we can see the terms here of a particular incident, on the basis of your verbal request for a statement, a request being made on the 8th of August. We can see the detail there. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, perhaps unnecessary to remind you that this document is under seal, will not be shown to the public, but will you please keep this in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We won't go into the detail of the document. But we can see it's an example of what you have said in relation to reports being sent as a result of a request and informing General Cermak about such a matter. There it is. We have no need to go into that any -- any further. And I'm not going to re-tread old ground. On another matter now, and it concerns page 254 of your report where you refer to the suggestion that General Cermak has the authority to investigate crimes and/or other irregular acts or order such investigations. And this arises from paragraph C in your report on that page, and it -- it concerns that aspect where he is the principal point of contact for the international community. Is it right that this proposition by you is based on the statements made by General Cermak to the international community that matters would be investigated or considered or they would -- that -- that he would report to them in relation to crimes or matters involving crimes that they had brought to his attention?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, it is based on -- on letters have I seen -- I have seen letters signed by General Cermak where he makes such a commitment, and, for example, in P1147 he writes that he has ordered the military police to conduct an investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah. Whether he can in law, can you provide any authority for that, within the legal provisions of the Croatian state at the time, whether he actually had, in law, the authority to investigate someone who was not a subordinate, because Article 19 of the Code of Military Discipline, which we looked at on the first day of my cross-examination with you, concerns subordinates. But in law, whether what he is saying, whether -- whether there is any authority for that.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are various Articles in the Code of Discipline that indicate that the commander, including the garrison commander, has the -- for example, the duty to collect or to take all measures to collect evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Shall we look at that first. Which Article are you citing?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Let's go to Article 61.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we have Exhibit P1007 on the screen, please, and if it could be put to page 16 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I put it to you about a subordinate, and that's what this Article refers to. "On learning of a disciplinary violation by a subordinate, the superior officer in the position of company commander, corresponding position or higher, must immediately take all necessary measures to collect relevant evidence and inform his superior officer." And so that concerns the subordinate. Under Article -- that is a disciplinary violation by a subordinate. If we go to Article 19, page 7: "Superior officers shall decide disciplinary responsibility of their subordinates ..." And we can see what that refers to. We dealt with this at the beginning of cross-examination, and I don't want to repeat over old ground if there's no need for it, and that concerns disciplinary measures. These are terms known to us. Shall I put a matter to you and deal with it, or do you have anything --

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to add something.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously when General Cermak received these letters from members of the international community, most of the letters I have seen, the alleged perpetrators were not identified, except for it was said members of the HV or somebody in military uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I agree with you that Article 61, for example, as it is there, only covers subordinates. But I would expect that somebody with the rank, experience, and in the position of General Cermak, being aware of the negative impact these letters from the international community could have on the image of Croatia would, during his contacts with General Gotovina, for example, or another operational commander in the area raise the matter, also raise the matter with the military police. And even if it was not established that this was a subordinate of his, which, based on the overall structure would be unlikely that it was a subordinate of his, still use his authority in order to achieve the desired result, i.e., to have the complaint by the members of the international community investigated, and also, obviously, the appropriate measures taken against the perpetrators, if the complaint was confirmed by the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Crimes are not disciplinary violations, are they?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But the same principles apply.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is there any other Article you would like to point out to us? I have pointed out Article 19, Article 26, Articles 6 and 10. We've just looked at 61. It's a matter of law in many respects, but it's just -- and I'm conscious of that. But ...

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Article 32 could also apply, but that would, of course, that is the right to arrest perpetrators, but that, of course, implies the perpetrator has been identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, and one has got to be careful about pointing things out. It's the circumstances to which the provisions apply as well which require consideration. Other than that, there's only the general duty of the public under Croatian law, which -- have you considered that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was actually thinking also of the regulations that apply to -- or that determine the duties of garrison commanders, i.e., that they are responsible for maintaining order and discipline in the area covered by the garrison. And crimes can affect order and discipline, in particular, if no action undertaken against the perpetrator, once he or she has been identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
