utterances.text: We've looked at that last week, and that concerns his orders, the garrison orders that are issued for order and discipline. Remember, we looked at the 30-kilometres per hour speed limit over the bridge. And those are his orders and rules that a garrison commander may make, which may permit the enforcement of those local rules.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is -- that is one example. And again, I have not seen specific rules being issued by General Cermak in relation to the kind of crimes we're talking about here. However, in D59 he speaks to the media about these crimes. I would expect, again, based on the doctrine that as a garrison commander, in particular, somebody with his rank, he would indeed issue rules in order to prevent the kind of activities he seriously criticised in a press Article, D59, and then we could look into D34, which -- which lists all kind of things or measures a garrison commander can take or has to take, and there is, for example, Article 17 on maintaining order and discipline; Article 28 on the obligation to hold a monthly review of the situation regarding work, order, and discipline.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I mean, we've looked at all those at the beginning, and I'm not going to go over those again. Garrison commanders can only deal with disciplinary measures and not disciplinary violations, as we looked at, at the beginning of my cross-examination, if you remember.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- you would have to refresh my memory with the Article of the Code of Discipline. But, I mean, common sense would clearly indicate that a garrison commander, especially somebody in a position of General Cermak at the time we are talking about and in the area we're talking about, would not kind of try to -- to hide behind an article and say, Oh, it is not my problem. But instead would be more proactive and actually do what he has been doing in his responses to the letters of complaint by members of the international community.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In a way, these are findings of fact for the Trial Chamber you're entering into it, aren't you, Mr. Theunens, to be frank. I am a little bit concerned because this is an matter of judgement here in relation to many details of the evidence that you may not -- not have.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly do not want to overstep the subject matter I have been requested to address. But my answer is based on my own military education and training, my understanding of Croatian armed forces doctrine as well as my review of the documents covering, in this particular case, the activities of General Cermak as the commander of the Knin garrison between the 6th of August, 1995 and November 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We've looked at the Articles of the Code of Military Discipline. You've pointed out those Articles that -- that apply. We've seen them. We can interpret them. But I was asking you, and you say you would expect a person of this rank to do this, that, or the other. There are a lot of pre-conditions to that. I'm just asking you to point out within the regulations if there was anything that supported that proposition any further to what we've looked at.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe I have answered the question. We have address add number of Articles from the Code of Discipline as well as the specific regulation D34 applying to the garrison commander, and I gave additional information which is not included in the regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah. So we've looked at all those -- those matters. Very well. I think that that I covers all matters I need ask you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that concludes my cross-examination of Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Theunens. Sorry for detaining you for so long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is no need to apologise, Mr. Kay. The Chamber expects to you prepare the lists of bar table documents in accordance with the items the Chamber has given. And I see that the furniture is already moving. Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not asking you to report to the Chamber about the result of you considering one day or one day plus. I just put on the record that Mr. Kay took less him that than he indicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I am aware of, and I will take to consider this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, you will be cross-examined by Mr. Mikulicic. Mr. Mikulicic is counsel for Mr. Markac. Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Allow me to go back to the start of your testimony in this courtroom which was on the 1st of December, when in reply to Mr. President's question, and I'm referring to transcript page 12879, line 20, you said, and I will quote the question by His Honour Judge Orie: "[In English] [Previous translation continues] ... in these proceedings, if you can explain that. [Interpretation] Your answer was [In English]: "My subject of expertise is that I'm familiar with command and control issues in the armed forces, as well as with the aspects of the conflict in former Yugoslavia which are relevant in the context of this proceedings." [Interpretation] You do remember both the question and the answer, don't you?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Would you like to add anything to your answer?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe I could use -- I could specify the use of the term "armed forces" in a sense to expand it, that it also covers the Croatian special police, which is not a formal part of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Would you like to add anything on the issue of the military, judiciary, and disciplinary proceedings within the Ministry of Interior and the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not specifically, except for the fact that I have not been able to locate a specific regulation that covers the enforcement of discipline within the special police. I don't know whether such a regulation exists, but I would expect such a regulation to exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can document number 1D62-0001 be called, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, in actual fact, the document has to do with the Article which again has to do with the lecture you held in Oslo on the 13th of January. Do you recall the Article in question? I'm referring to page 6 where you speak of the role of the military expertise in -- at trial, and there you quote from the English dictionary what an UN expert represents. In other words, it's an individual who is skillful and has great knowledge of an issue. You go on to cite the jurisprudence of the Tribunal, where you say that an expert witness is a person, who has some specialized knowledge, skill, or training, and can assist a Trial Chamber in understanding an issue in dispute. Presumably, Mr. Theunens, you still hold this view that this is, indeed, what an expert witness should represent.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And the footnotes are there to identify -- yeah, to identify the sources of these entries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well. I'm referring you to page 8 of the document, where you said that the role of a military expert, and here you're referring to an expert coming from the Prosecution, is to become acquainted with the evidence at the disposal of the Prosecution. Does this mean, Mr. Theunens, that evidence, other documents -- or, rather, documents other than the ones that are at the disposal of the Prosecution need not be the subject of expertise?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not what the text says. I think you have to look at the text also from a practical point of view. That is, that, to my knowledge, internal expert reports are filed long before the trial starts, which means that the internal expert has had no access to documents provided by the Defence. As I mentioned during my testimony based on questions I believe by Mr. Kay, but also from what you will find further on in the article, in my view -- sorry. In my view, it would -- or it's a proposal that I make it would be good if the expert could have access to all the material the parties, i.e., Defence and Prosecution, and maybe also the Trial Chamber, once him or her to review and is not being called as an expert for the Defence or "for the Prosecution," but as an expert of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You've already explained that to us, Mr. Theunens. I would like to ask you this. When you quoted documents such as the legislation of the Republic of Croatia, which were in possession of the Prosecution, did you also have the occasion to review the legislation that was not part of the material provided to you by the Prosecution? In other words, some other regulations, governing a certain issue; for instance, disciplinary procedures within the Ministry of Interior or the Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I mentioned, I had expected to have access to a regulation, a specific regulation for the special police defining discipline within the special police as well as responsibilities of commanders to enforce it as well as the different types of breaches of violations. I have not come across such a regulation. As far as what Ministry of Defence, it is my understanding that the Code of Discipline -- the Military Code of Discipline as well as the other documents I have cited were applicable -- or were still into effect during and after Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, on the 1st of December at the start of your testimony, transcript page 12871, line 19, you said [In English]: "A legal expert, so I am not familiar with the details of the international law in the relation to the authority of the -- of a commander or the responsibility of a commander on the occupational regime." [Interpretation] My understanding of this is that you do not perceive yourself as an expert witness for law, and here you highlighted international law. Did you study domestic law or comparative law, in relation to the topic of your expertise here?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would just like to clarify first, okay, the commander on the occupational regime --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: At this time, this is of no interest to me, Mr. Theunens. Can you please answer my question: Did you study domestic or comparative law, although you initially stated that you were not a legal expert?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, you asked for a clarification about a part of the question, where you were quoted, talking about a commander or the responsibility of a commander on the occupational regime. If you'd like to give that clarification as part of your answer, you're allowed to do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, and I will do it very briefly. I am familiar with what is stipulated in the Geneva Conventions under belligerent occupation which would also cover the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm a little bit procedurally at a disadvantage here because is he now giving testimony about an issue that I covered with him and that Mr. Mikulicic is not covering with him. So if he gives an answer, it could be added to my time that I'm seeking for -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Mr. Theunens said that he would deal with it briefly. You'll get briefly an opportunity to deal with the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We'll see how briefly he deals with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll see.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are just two words to come. So it was which would also cover the operational commander first up. Coming back to Mr. Mikulicic's question, I have had private law, public law, trade law even, but that was in a separate course I attended, as well as obviously laws of armed convict. Some aspects of international law and that during the various stages of my military education, Military Academy first and then in particular during the one-year staff course I attended between 1997 -- 1998 and 1999, if I remember well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Theunens, do you know if the Geneva Conventions you have just mentioned were stipulated in the domicile law of the Republic of Croatia, in 1995; in other words, at the time of the events covered by the indictment?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are various regulations that -- I mean, military regulations that highlight the duties of a commander and also the members of the armed forces to abide by the laws of armed conflict. I just have a difficulty now to locate the exact formulation. Now, in addition, there is also -- I'm sorry. Yeah, I will find it during the break. There was, for example -- there is correspondence between General Tolj and the ICRC about training of members of the -- of the Croatian armed forces, in the international laws of war. I am -- I do not remember a specific reference in a Croatian law, even though military regulations have the character of a law for military personnel, but I don't remember a specific reference to the Geneva Conventions in the Croatian laws I reviewed. But I will check it certainly during the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: While you were preparing your expertise, did you review the Criminal Code of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember specifically reviewing the Criminal Code. I'm pretty sure I have seen it, but I have not included any references to it in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, did you study the organisation and structure of military courts in the Republic of Croatia, as you were preparing your expertise?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed. And those aspects -- or that aspect is covered in part 1 of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Just to make sure that there is no misunderstanding, I'm not referring to the disciplinary courts but the military courts that were established pursuant to the decrees of the president of the Republic and the Law on Courts. Did you review the work of the courts and the substantive and procedural law applied by the courts, the case law, the way in which the courts are regulated in terms of the work of the judges, and I'm likewise referring to the structure of the military prosecutor's offices. Did you study that topic?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed. And it is covered in part 1 of the report in the section of military law and military justice, and I have, indeed, made a distinction between disciplinary courts and disciplinary prosecutors as well as the military courts. And for the legal framework, for example, I can direct to you English pages or the section, excuse me, the section -- in section 7, title 7, subtitle A, legal framework, which can be found on English pages 203 to 211, where we also have information on military courts and military prosecutors.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In your view, Mr. Theunens, or, rather, a moment ago you talked about this. Can you tell what is your definition of the military judiciary? What does "military judiciary" mean to you?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It consists of a system that allows to investigate, prosecute, and as well put on trial crimes that are defined in the supporting legislation committed by military personnel, whereby as is addressed in this section, there exists a system of military prosecutors, military courts, and there are also procedures established that allow, for example, or that determine the authority of the military police in the investigation of such facts as well as determine the rights and duties of suspects who are being investigated, prosecuted, and put on trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, is it your view that the military judiciary was organised within the military authorities of the Republic of Croatia, or do you hold a different view?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is obvious that the military judiciary, i.e., the military prosecutor and the military court, are outside the chain of command in order to guarantee their independence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know how military prosecutors in the Republic of Croatia were organised?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the information I have on that topic can be found in part 1 of the report, pages 205 to 208, where there's reference made to the relevant legal stipulations. And, for example, I mention, and this comes from 65 ter 828, that there is a military state prosecutor's office in Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the military prosecutor in Split. Who was the military prosecutor in Split subordinated to? Or any other military prosecutor in the territory of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know for sure that they're not subordinated to the operational commander. I would expect them to be subordinated through the judicial structure to the -- a supreme type of prosecutor in Zagreb, but I don't have specific information on that in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The supreme prosecutor in Zagreb you're referring to, was he a civilian or a military prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I should like to call up D906, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, when this is prepared, I'm looking at the clock, I would like to have a break within the next two to seven minutes, if you could find a suitable moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, maybe it will be convenient to have a break immediately because I'm just entering into the theme that will show up other documents on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That was the reason why I asked you to consider it. Apart from that one of your first questions referred to transcript page 12879, where you also see how easily a mistake is made where you said that the witness answered the question put by me to him about his field of expertise, and he remembered the question and the answer. Mr. Kay might be a bit surprised that the questions he has put to the witness are put in my mouth now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: It is my mistake, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you also see that questions with small implications, the witness said he remembered that. I find it difficult to accept that Mr. Theunens remembered a question being put to him by me if was actually Mr. Kay. I'm not expressing myself on what are the better questions. I leave that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The subject of the question was an issue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The subject of the question was approximately the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have a break, and we resume at five minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, I was informed that you'd like to clarify one of the answers you gave earlier. I will give you an opportunity to do so, although it appears that you're developing habits and customs at the beginning an end of the sessions as well. Yes, about the Geneva Conventions, at least I was told that was something that you would like to say something about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, and I don't want to develop this into a bad habit, but just to clarify that the answer to Mr. Mikulicic's question can be found on English page 188 in part 1 of the report, when I quote from the 1993 presidential decision on the amendment to the service regulations of the armed forces which is P1117, so 1117. And Article 250 of this exhibit explicitly mentions the Geneva Conventions, and, of course, 251 and 252 as well as 253, i.e., the Articles of P1117 are also relevant in this context. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mikulicic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now that you have mentioned the Geneva Conventions, my question was put in a slightly different manner. I was interested in whether you are familiar with the procedure used to incorporate the Geneva Conventions and The Hague Protocols as well as other international regulations, into the body of the Croatian law.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not familiar with that specific procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Perhaps you can recall something if I told you that the Geneva Conventions were ratified by the Croatian parliament and pursuant to that act, they became part of domestic law in Croatia, automatically being implemented. A part of the Geneva Conventions had earlier been incorporated into the penal code of the Republic of Croatia. Does this jog your memory in any way?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not specifically, Your Honours. I have not looked into that legal matter in detail, but I have no reason to doubt about what Mr. Mikulicic just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, while we have this document on the screen I would like to draw your attention on the topic that has been raised while testimonying [sic] Mr. Zeljko Zganjer. I draw attention to the wrong translation of the Croatian word vojni sud military court, that has been wrongly translation as a court martial. We are still waiting for the official translating -- for the official translation, and for that purpose, I will use this documents but having in mind this objection on the wrong translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please keep that in mind that whenever reference is made to vojni sud that you should understand this for the question to be military court or perhaps military judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Or military prosecutor, whatever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Theunens, are you familiar with this document that is on the screen?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I have quoted from this decree on English page 208 of part 1 of the report as well as on the following pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If I may then, I'd like to go through the document, in particular Article 2 says that in case of imminent threat of war and with the aim of preserving independence and integrity of the Republic of Croatia, all courts shall continue their work. Paragraph 2 refers to military courts being established. Article 6 speaks of the jurisdiction of military courts. Did you study what the substantial law is that was supposed to be applied by military courts?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, substantive law.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have addressed the military courts, i.e., the legislation, in very general terms just to -- in order to establish that there were military courts. I also described their mandate or the jurisdiction, i.e., Article 6, where reference is made to the SFRY Criminal Code. And then I have also included some reference to Article 3 and 4. I have not done any further research or analysis on the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we agree, Mr. Theunens, that military courts did not apply any particular or separate area of the law and that they, rather, applied the penal code provisions that were in force in the Republic of Croatia at that time?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is my understanding of -- of Article 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If we look at Article 7 on the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have that on the screen. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If we look at Article 7 we see that district courts have jurisdiction to decide on appeals against military courts' decisions made in the first instance by a military judge. The district courts referred to in Article 7, are those also military courts or civilian courts?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, as the text indicates, these are civilian courts, the text in Article 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Article 8: "The Supreme Court of the Republic of Croatia has jurisdiction to decide on appeals" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, you quoted Article 7, and I'm -- you said that: "We see that district courts have jurisdiction to decide on appeals against military courts' decisions made in the first instance by a military judge," whereas I read that it's a single judge, and I take it then that it's a single judge in a military court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But it's a single judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: It's a single judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That's was not what you put to the witness. You said by military judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Well, okay. In fact, this is a single judge in a first instance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I think the witness then answered your question, that it was a civilian court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have the same question in relation to Article 8: "The Supreme Court of the Republic of Croatia had jurisdiction to decide on appeals against military Court decisions made in first instance by judicial Chambers." You will agree that the Supreme Court of the Republic of Croatia is also a civilian court?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours, that's what the Article says.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: As we can see in Article 6 of the decree that the military courts applied provisions of the penal code. Procedurally speaking, do you know what law was used by military courts? Was it a separate law or the same law that was in place encompassing all courts in the Republic of Croatia at the time?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, when we see Article 6, there's only reference made to the Criminal Code of Croatia, which, actually there was a SFRY Criminal Code of 1991 which was adopted by Croatia, and I'm not aware of the existence of separate legislation that would be applied in this context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I think that Mr. Mikulicic, although he first referred to the substantive law to be applied, was asking about law of procedure. If I understood you well, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please -- procedurally speaking, do you know what law was used by military courts. I understood this to be law of procedure.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no specific knowledge of which -- of what procedural law the military courts applied.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Article 11 mentions the way judges are elected, as regards military courts. It is stated here that per establishment, they are assigned by the defence minister upon the minister of judiciary's proposal and the administration for among the ranks of municipal and district court judges. Could you please comment.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the Article is clear. In my report I also include a reference to Article 10 which deals with the composition of the military court but also decisions to increase the number of the judges, and there it is stated that the decision shall be made by the minister of justice and public administration acting on the proposal of the president of the military court. So, indeed, we see the role played by the minister of justice in this aspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the fact that the military court judges were supposed to be elected from among the ranks of the Croatian army; that is to say, the Ministry of Defence? Do you have any knowledge as regards that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no specific -- or no particular knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask the registrar to put up D907 next.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, you will see a decision on appointment of a particular military judge being assigned to the military court in Split. I also wanted to draw the Chamber's attention on the wrong translation, what is discussed here are -- is not court-martial but military courts. You can see in the preamble that on the proposal of the minister of the judiciary, the Minister of Defence decides on the appointment and disposition of the judges at the Split military court, where two judges were being appointed as per establishment. Previously they had been judges at the municipal court in Split. Do you agree with me, that this was an operational way to implement the decree we saw in Exhibit D906 and that the military court is being replenished with the judges of civilian courts?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, that is what the document states.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's have a look at D908 next.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: It is the Law on Courts, one of the basic bodies of law in the Republic of Croatia, regulating the structure of courts in the Republic of Croatia. As stated in Article 1, it regulates the structure, jurisdiction, and scope of activity of the courts. If we go to page 2, in particular, Article 13, we see that the judiciary is being organised in Croatia to be organised at the level of municipal courts, county courts, military courts, commercial courts, the higher commercial court of the Republic of Croatia, the administrative court of the Republic of Croatia, and the highest judicial instance in the Republic of Croatia is the Supreme Court. Mr. Theunens, in the course of drafting your report, did you study the structure of courts in the Republic of Croatia, their authority and subject matter, jurisprudence, as well as any potential differences that may have existed between the military and civilian courts in the course of 1995? Was this a subject of -- or topic of your interest?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. I have not addressed the issues raised by Mr. Mikulicic, except for the entries on the military courts which can be found on -- between English pages 208 to 211 in part 1 of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In the course of your training and education, did you have occasion to study up close the system of courts in any other country that would have a system different to that of the Republic of Croatia? Did you have occasion to view this topic comparatively?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am familiar with the system in my own country, including court-martials where even sat in what we call a court-martial while I was serving in the Brussels garrison, but otherwise, I have not done any comparative analysis or similar study between the Belgian including legal, including military legal system, and other legal system. Systems I have -- as I said, I have not studied the Croatian legal system, except for the aspects on military courts and military prosecutors which are addressed in part 1 of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Since you have mentioned court-martial, in your expert view, do you think there is a difference, and if there is, what it is, as opposed to a military court?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would have to look at the legislation and then see whether any distinction or -- excuse me, first see what name is being used and then see whether any distinction is made between the two. In my own country the military court was the most supreme military judicial institution, which would, for example, deal with appeals, whereas court-martial was the first level of military -- yeah, one would say court, but military judicial institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The courts you have referred to in your country, are they part of the civilian judiciary or the military structure?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just for your information, the system in my country has been abolished or at least suspended, so it is not active anymore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, at an earlier stage, I have expressed my concern about side roads before we go into the history of the Belgian system, which has meanwhile been abolished, and whether these were civilian where Belgian appears to be just one example of which the expert, I take it mainly because he is of Belgian nationality, appears to have some knowledge. I don't know whether that whether assist the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Obviously that's not an expert knowledge. That is my point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That point is clear to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask for the 65 ter document 00465 to be brought up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the document - there it is - it is a regulation that was put in force towards the end of 1996. First of all, Mr. Theunens, did you have occasion to see this document before?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, and I'm under the impression that -- I have used it in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well. This document abolished certain regulation in the area of the judiciary that had been passed during the state of war and imminent threat of war. By the way, Mr. Theunens, do you have any knowledge of whether a state of war was ever declared in the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe that such a state was declared in 1991. However, I don't know whether the state that existed in 1991 was ever abolished or whether it was re-declared -- I mean declared again at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Would you be surprised, Mr. Theunens, if I told you that there was never a state of war proclaimed in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not be surprised. I mean, it's not a matter I have looked into or analysed from a particular -- or analysed, so, yeah, I do believe you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If we look at this particular decree invalidating the 1991 decrees, we will see, under Article 2, that all the cases heard by the military courts are to be remanded to the competent municipal or district courts as well as the cases that military prosecutors offices were seized of were to be transferred back to the competent municipal or district prosecutors. I think we will agree, Mr. Theunens, that the structure of military courts was abolished, and that the cases not completed before the military courts were being transferred to the competent civilian courts. Will you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed that is what the document states, and I have included a summary of this decree on English pages 204, 205 of part 1 of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Similarly, presidents of military courts, judges of military courts, and military prosecutors and their deputies, through the invalidation of 1991 decrees, were transferred back to the posts that they had earlier occupied in courts or prosecutor's offices. We initially saw that that was indeed where the military courts were staffed from. When we look at the relevant legislation, will you agree with me, Mr. Theunens, that we cannot speak of a military judiciary in the Republic of Croatia but rather of specialized courts which heard cases on the basis of civilian legal provisions. Based on a civilian procedure, they heard cases on certain acts or matters for which they were granted jurisdiction by the law?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I will repeat it. Will you agree with me that the so-called military courts were, in fact, a type of specialized courts which, at a concern point in time, were set up within the civilian judiciary or civilian justice administration in the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's probably the case. I mean, I have not done any legal analysis on how the military court system was established and what its relation was with the civilian court system or judicial system. All I did was include the most relevant legal references in relation to military courts and military prosecutors in part 1 of my report. It's just a kind of an enumeration without any analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I would like to tender this documented into evidence, Your Honour. 65 ter 465.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be exhibit number D01076.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are now in the 10.000s, which I would not --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: A little bit too much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- try to support. Mr. Registrar, may I take it that it is 1076. I have to look at the --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That is absolutely correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is not easy to fill in halfway. D1076 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Mikulicic, may I briefly ask you one of the previous documents I find several times, including the documents where you state that the translations are not in every respect correct. It says courtesy translation. Comes as a bit of a surprise to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We didn't find a better bay way to depict the document. It was translationed [sic] by the Defence, and was only done for the purposes of a particular witness. In the meantime, we ask for official translations, and we ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear to me, and further, the bureau for statistics dealing with -- be at the heading of military legislation is that a mistake, or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No that is so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That doesn't resolve a puzzle for me, because you make selections from the piece of legislation, but at the top we still find that although it is signed by the president, it is published by the bureau of statistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that is why we need a legal expert to explore all this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Statistical aspects are for -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I wonder whether we can [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Theunens, as part of preparations for your expertise, did you review the jurisprudence and application of the law before military courts in a comparative overview in relation to the civilian courts? And I'm referring to the type of criminal policies, types of sanctions, the use of detention, et cetera. Did you study that sort of topic?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, I have not made such a comparison covering the aspects enumerated by Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was an area of your interest the courts within the Ministry of the Interior --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can Mr. Mikulicic please repeat what sort of courts those were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, you're invited by the interpreters to repeat what kind of courts you had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I had in mind disciplinary court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Disciplinary courts --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Of the Ministry of Interior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of the Ministry of Interior.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is one of the aspects I highlighted in the beginning, that I didn't have access to a specific regulation on discipline within the Ministry of Interior or even that applied to the special police. So I would -- I wanted to have a look at that and study it, but I did not come across such a document or regulation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could we pull up 65 ter 1182.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Theunens, you have the Official Gazette of the Republic of Croatia before you, issue number 29, of 1991. This issue published the Law on Internal Affairs. Did you have the occasion to study the Law?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just checking whether I made any references to it. I have not made any references to this Law. I mean, I have a reference to the May 1991 Law on Amendment of the 1989 Law on Internal Affairs which can be found on English page 102 of part 1 of the report, and it seems -- it seems to be the same 65 ter, so maybe I'm confused here. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whatever the case may be, can Mr. Registrar help us and show us Article 80 of the Law, which deals disciplinary responsibility. That's page 154.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The Law on Internal Affairs that we have before us now in the provisions of chapter 5 which deal with disciplinary responsibility regulates the disciplinary courts and their procedure within the Ministry of the Interior. Thus, Article 81 envisages -- [In English] [Previous translation continues] ... another page in Croatian and 155 in English. [Interpretation] Article 81 envisages that minor infractions of military discipline shall be regulated in a general regulation and that the decision to initiate proceedings shall be rendered by the minister of the interior or an official authorised to do so by the minister. Did you review the provisions on military responsibility and the military procedure within the Ministry of Interior?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The transcript says military responsibility, but I assume you mean disciplinary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Disciplinary responsibility, of course. It is a mistake. Thank you for your remark.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have reviewed the law, but I have no recollection that I reviewed this specific Articles, and I have not included them in my report, whereas, based on your question, I should have included them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Article 82 relates to major offences of work discipline, and I draw your attention to item or point 14 which speaks of a criminal offence as a major breach of work discipline, and I believe we will be discussing that tomorrow. Article 82, last paragraph, reads that the proposal for initiating a disciplinary procedure for a major breach of work discipline shall be submitted by the Minister of the Interior or a person authorised by him for that purpose. Article 83 reads that the proceedings shall be initiated, and the disciplinary court shall render a decision thereupon. Are you familiar with the work of the disciplinary courts within the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. I'm not familiar with the work of the disciplinary courts within the Ministry of Interior of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, when you put Article 81 to the witness, and let me quote you literally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's 75 page -- line 24.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. You said, "Article 81 envisages that minor infractions of military discipline shall be regulated in a general regulation." I'm just trying to find that in Article 81. Could you assist me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: It's paragraph 1 in Article 81 and the Croatian words opci akt has been translated that way. I'm not very sure whether this is a really --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have difficulties in finding the word "military."

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No military at all.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction. It may have been an interpreter's mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A couple of times your words have been translated as referring not only to work discipline but to military discipline, and I was just informed by the interpreters that there may have been interpretation mistakes. So whenever you referred to discipline in this context, I do understand that you referred to work discipline and not to military discipline.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... and within the Ministry of Interior, so it has nothing to do with a military or the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I was just confused by --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the way in which it appeared on our transcript, and I thought it wise not to suffer under this confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: It probably, Your Honour, it is my mistake, but it is quite difficult to follow the transcript on one side, on the other side [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not blaming you. I have to do a job as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Article 83 provides for serious infringements of work discipline, and provides for a first instance disciplinary court to be set up in every police administration and in the seat of the ministry as well. Article 84 goes on to speak of the first instance, disciplinary court consisting of a president and two members; and the second instance, court of a president and four members. Do you know, Mr. Theunens, what sort of substantive and procedural law was applied by the disciplinary courts of the Ministry of Interior?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. This is not a matter I have addressed in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In other words, your expertise on the matter cannot help us here, if my understanding is correct.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I take it that you -- your answer is that have you no specific expertise on the matter and that did you not study it when preparing your report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is -- that's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Theunens, a moment ago you said that unfortunately you did not have occasion to review the regulations regulating the disciplinary responsibility of the police, including members of the special police. I would like to direct your attention to Article 24 of the Law, regulating the establishment of the special police. Can you agree with me that the special police, its structure, and the reason why it was set up can be found among the provisions of the Law on Internal Affairs that we've just looked at?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours, and I have mentioned or addressed Article 24 on page 103 of part 1 of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: May this document be made an evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D1077. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Exhibit D1077 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Law that we have just looked at was amended in October 1994. I am referring you to Exhibit P1148. We will get back to that later.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean the October 1994 amendment can be found on English pages -- at least the relevant sections on special police on English pages 103 and 104 of part 1 of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, in your expert opinion, can you tell us and describe for us what the basic difference is between the disciplinary courts, which, as we were able to see were set up within the Ministry of Interior, and the regular civilian courts, which were set up pursuant to the Law on Courts of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have not reviewed the Articles 80 to 85 of the -- of Exhibit D1077, so I'm not in a position to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You will remember that we said that decisions on serious breaches of work discipline and disciplinary proceedings will be passed -- or, rather, the decisions to initiate such proceedings will be passed by the Ministry of the Interior or another person authorised by him to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we call up 3D01-0723?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: This is a decision dated March 1995 of the Ministry of the Interior rendered by the assistant minister, Mr. Mladen Markac, whereby Mario Spekuljuk was suspended from duty as a member of the special police anti-terrorist unit Lucko. Let me ask you first if you have ever had the occasion to see this document?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In the preamble of the decision, Mr. Markac, who rendered the decision invokes the powers under Articles 89 and 90 of the Law on Internal Affairs we have just looked at. Article 90 says that a decision on the suspension from duty can be rendered by the minister or somebody authorised by him to do so, and Article 89 says that a member of the Ministry of the Interior may be suspended from duty when a criminal procedure has been initiated against him. It follows from this decision, Mr. Theunens, that an investigation had been launched against Mario Spekuljuk for the perpetration of the crime of soliciting prostitutes and that an investigating judge had ordered an investigation against that person. Mr. Theunens, what are your comments, in relation to the way this decision was passed or to the decision itself?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have only this document in front of me, but it -- it appears that General Markac is exercising his authority in line with -- and also fulfilling his duties in line with what is stipulated in the Law on Internal Affairs and more specifically the Articles dealing with enforcing discipline and acting against people who have violated discipline.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Correct. I agree with you, Mr. Theunens. Can we agree that it clearly follows from this document that General Markac received information that against a member of the anti-terrorist unit of Lucko, a criminal procedure had been initiated and that detention was ordered whereby a decision for the suspension of duty was passed in this particular specific case?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I just see the bottom of the document, because --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could I have a number for this document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be D1078, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1078 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I have just one more document, Your Honour, and that will be -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are close to -- one document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: One document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One or two minutes, not more, because otherwise -- okay, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] Can we have document P609, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, we've seen the document whereby Mr. Markac suspended from duty a member of the special police against whom a criminal proceedings were launched. We have on our screen a document which shows that Mr. Markac addressed the commander of the unit Mario Spekuljuk was a member of as a specialist, and that is the anti-terrorist unit Lucko, and that he delivered the decision on suspension from duty. Will you agree with me that this, in fact, is the implementation of the measures contained in the decision that is now exhibited as D1078?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it is, and P609 is also mentioned in the addendum. It would have been good if D1078 would also have been included there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That concludes my examination for today, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we adjourn for the day, the Chamber would inform the parties about its decision it has taken in respect of the defendant Ante Gotovina's request to reply to the Prosecution's response to Gotovina's notice concerning the addendum to Colonel Konings's expert report, which was filed the 9th of December, and since it is a urgent matter, the Chamber, although not yet impressed by the reasons given and still considering to what extent the assumptions in this request or the implications as described in it, and what to rely upon and what not to rely upon, still considering all that, the Chamber has decided that it uses its discretion to allow the Gotovina Defence to -- to reply but orally not more than five minutes, and then an opportunity will be given to do so tomorrow. I can -- I take it that you'd rather not have it earlier in the mourn, but take as much time as possible. But, of course, we can't just postpone Konings' matters eternally. Therefore, we have used the discretion to at least grant, perhaps not in full because I take that you in mind to address the matter in writing, but at least to grant it partially by giving you an opportunity to address the issues that you wanted to address in five minutes in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So I take it, Your Honour, you just want to hear our reply not to not the whole matter, just a five-minute reply orally to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And as I said earlier, the Chamber has seriously considered whether to grant at all. We finally reached the decision that's what I said, not yet being impressed by the argument raised, but using its discretion will not disallow, will not deny the motion in its entirety and give an opportunity. If after these five minutes, or course, the Chamber will take a totally different view, then, of course, we would reconsider the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, we would like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.00, and I have to address Mr. Registrar to know for sure in which courtroom, otherwise you will find out. I hardly ever would send an expert or a witness home and say, Try to find out in what courtroom we're in tomorrow. But you're one of the exceptions, Mr. Theunens. You will certainly be able with the assistance of the victims and witness section, no one else, of course, to find out where we would like to see you back. It's Courtroom I, as Mr. Misetic tells me, and which is confirmed with the registrar, so you don't need a sleepless night for that reason alone. We would like to see you back at 9.00 tomorrow morning. I, again, instruct you that you should not speak with anyone about the testimony already given or still to be given, and we adjourn until tomorrow, the 10th of December, 9.00, Courtroom I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 10th day of December, 2008, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.05 p.m.,
